**Summary.** This paper presents detailed numerical simulations on cooling and trapping fast ortho-positronium atoms using laser cooling techniques. By modeling the system's quantum evolution via the master equation, the authors demonstrate that simultaneous deceleration, cooling, and trapping are highly feasible with current technology. The results pave the way for creating ultra-cold Ps ensembles for advanced quantum physics experiments.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work tackles the complex open quantum system dynamics of a purely leptonic system (Ps) under strong laser fields, providing detailed numerical protocols for achieving ultra-cold quantum states relevant for fundamental QED tests.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study numerically investigates the laser deceleration, cooling, and trapping of fast ortho-positronium (Ps) bunches.

**Main result.** The authors confirm very good prospects for simultaneously achieving deceleration, cooling, and optical trapping of Ps atoms using standard Doppler cooling geometries, even incorporating higher transitions.

**Method.** The research employs advanced numerical simulations solving the Lindblad master equation using a semi-classical approach and Monte Carlo wave function simulation (MCWFS).

**Model / system.** The system is ortho-positronium (o-Ps), a pure QED object, whose evolution is modeled using the Lindblad master equation. The simulation incorporates the full Zeeman manifold and extends to include higher transitions ($2^3P-3^3D$).

**Key observables.** Final kinetic temperature, fraction of non-annihilated atoms, and the time evolution of momentum and density.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Laser pulse energies ($	ext{mJ}$), durations ($\approx 100 	ext{ ns}$), and specific detunings/Rabi frequencies for the transitions.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis uses a semi-classical description for atomic motion and assumes the initial source is a fast, hot cloud of Ps atoms.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the quantum states of the Zeeman manifold and show the time evolution of physical parameters, comparing results from running-wave versus standing-wave laser fields.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical framework (master equation, semi-classical force) to presenting extended numerical studies confirming feasibility, and finally discussing future enhancements using optical cavities.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We numerically study laser deceleration, cooling and trapping of host fast ortho-positronium (Ps) bunches as produced in silica microchannel targets using positron bunches from a Surko trap. While Doppler laser cooling routinely allows to cool neutral atom species below milli-Kelvin kinetic temperatures, the fast ground state annihilation and the high recoil shift to line-width ratio in Ps pose new challenging limitations on timing and the required laser power. Earlier theoretical work and first experiments already exhibit viable prospects for radiation pressure cooling to create unprecedented cold and dense Ps ensembles. Our extended numerical studies confirm very good prospects to simultaneously decelerate, cool and optically trap Ps atoms in a standard Doppler cooling geometry on the $1^3\mathrm{S}$--$2^3\mathrm{P}$ transition. Including the full Zeeman state manifolds and adding additional transverse lasers on the $2^3\mathrm{P}$--$3^3\mathrm{D}$ transition improves timing and final temperature to allow for optical trapping at the end. The required laser powers and geometry parameters to implement effective slowing and trapping within a time frame, where the majority of atoms is not annihilated, is in reach of current technology of $\mathrm{mJ}$ energy pulses of approximately $100\ \mathrm{ns}$ duration. Future extensions to collectively enhance cooling and trapping in optical cavities or hollow-core fibres should finally allow fast preparation of ultra-cold Ps systems as future basis of superradiant lasing and Bose--Einstein condensates.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes how the breakdown of quantum simulation accuracy, known as the Trotterisation threshold, behaves when environmental noise and decoherence are present. Using three distinct physical models, the authors demonstrate that this threshold persists even in the steady state, confirming that the underlying unitary chaos dictates the simulation limit. They introduce RMT techniques to characterize the emergence of genuinely dissipative quantum chaos.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it bridges the gap between idealized closed-system quantum chaos theory and realistic open quantum systems, providing crucial diagnostics for assessing the feasibility of quantum simulation in noisy environments.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the persistence and nature of the 'Trotterisation threshold' in Digital Quantum Simulation (DQS) when open-system effects (environmental noise and decoherence) are included, and characterizes the emergence of quantum chaos in these open systems.

**Main result.** The Trotterisation threshold persists even in the long-time, steady-state limit of open systems, and dissipative quantum chaos emerges when dissipation balances underlying unitary quantum chaos.

**Method.** The authors use open-system DQS applied to three models, characterizing chaos using new statistical techniques based on Random Matrix Theory (RMT) applied to both unitary and dissipative regimes.

**Model / system.** The study examines open-system quantum simulators using the Lindblad master equation, applied to paradigmatic models including the quantum kicked top, the nearest-neighbour Heisenberg spin chain, and the Rabi model.

**Key observables.** Spin magnetization ($\langlear{J}_zangle$), qubit polarization ($\langle\sigma_1^zangle$), normalized photon number ($\langle nangle/n_j$), and simulation fidelity ($F$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Trotter step size ($	au$), dissipation rates ($\gamma_k$), and the dissipation scaling factor ($f_\gamma$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the Markovian dissipation approximation, and the threshold behavior is analyzed across varying dissipation strengths.

**Figures summary.** Figures show time evolution of observables and fidelity for the three models across varying dissipation strengths and Trotter step sizes, demonstrating the threshold's persistence in both time and steady-state regimes.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the DQS of three open systems, first establishing the persistence of the threshold in time-domain observables, then confirming this in steady-state fidelity measurements, and finally detailing the conditions for dissipative quantum chaos.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Digital quantum simulation (DQS) is one of the most promising applications of quantum computing. Trotterised DQS models quantum dynamics by decomposing the evolution into a sequence of gate-based Trotter steps. Using larger Trotter steps reduces the required gate count, but it is now understood that the Trotterisation step size cannot be increased beyond a certain threshold value, beyond which there is a sudden breakdown in simulation accuracy, due to the onset of quantum chaos. To date, this behaviour has only been studied for closed systems not subjected to the environmental noise and decoherence to which real-world quantum computers are highly sensitive. In this work, we study a range of experimentally relevant open-system quantum simulator models and show that Trotterisation thresholds persist even when open-system effects are included, even in the long-time, steady-state limit, once all coherence has been lost. We show that open DQS can accurately reproduce the dynamics of open target systems prior to the threshold, but still exhibits a sudden performance breakdown beyond it. We introduce new, statistical techniques to rigorously characterise the onset of quantum chaos beyond the Trotterisation threshold for both approximately unitary and genuine dissipative quantum chaos, based on random matrix theory (RMT), building on techniques developed for closed systems. Finally, we demonstrate that dissipative quantum chaos emerges when the dissipation is in balance with the presence of underlying unitary quantum chaos; the dissipation must be strong enough to induce genuinely dissipative behaviour, yet not so strong as to suppress the underlying chaotic structure.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper develops a quantitative theory to calculate electron decoherence when an electron passes through nanoscale apertures or holes. By using advanced electromagnetic techniques, the authors derive expressions for decoherence probability in both cylindrical and circular geometries. The findings are crucial for designing next-generation coherent electron-beam instruments by quantifying how environmental coupling limits imaging resolution.

**Why it may be interesting.** The rigorous treatment of decoherence using full electromagnetic response and retardation is highly relevant to open quantum systems, particularly those involving nanoscale confinement or structured environments where environmental coupling is critical.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses how electron decoherence, caused by interaction with the environment, fundamentally limits the resolution and contrast in phase-sensitive electron microscopy.

**Main result.** The authors derived quantitative theories for decoherence in cylindrical holes and circular apertures, finding that for large holes, decoherence can dominate spatial broadening, necessitating its inclusion in instrument design.

**Method.** The methodology combines an electromagnetic Green-tensor formulation with the fluctuation-dissipation theorem, fully retaining retardation effects to calculate the decoherence probability and elastic phase.

**Model / system.** The study models electron wave propagation through two canonical geometries: a cylindrical hole drilled through a metal and a circular aperture in a thin conducting film. The interaction is treated via the minimal-coupling Hamiltonian.

**Key observables.** Decoherence probability ($P$), elastic phase ($\chi$), and the resulting visibility of interference patterns.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Temperature ($T$), conductivity ($\sigma$), aperture radius ($a$), and the electron trajectory position.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis uses the nonrecoil approximation and assumes the environment is in thermal equilibrium. Previous work often failed to account for full retardation or curved boundaries.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the physical setups (cylindrical hole vs. aperture) and show how decoherence probability varies with temperature and path separation, comparing full calculations against simplified approximations.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops a quantitative theory by first establishing the Green-tensor framework, then deriving specific closed-form expressions for the cylindrical hole and the circular aperture, and finally comparing the resulting decoherence effects.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The coherence of free electrons sets fundamental limits on the resolution and contrast of phase-sensitive electron microscopy because coherence is lost whenever the electron leaves a distinguishing excitation in its environment. We develop a quantitative theory of fast-electron decoherence in two canonical geometries: a cylindrical hole drilled through a realistic metal and a circular aperture in a thin perfectly conducting film. By combining an electromagnetic Green-tensor formulation with the fluctuation--dissipation theorem while fully retaining retardation, we obtain the decoherence probability and elastic phase as functions of the electron trajectory, temperature, and material response. For the cylindrical hole, we obtain a closed-form, azimuthally resolved expression that separates the dependences on path position, temperature, and conductivity. In the high-conductivity and high-temperature limits, this result reduces to a universal expression that is linear in temperature and independent of both conductivity and electron velocity. For the circular aperture, which we solve using a cylindrical-wave modal expansion, the energy-loss probability diverges as $1/ω$ at low frequency, whereas the decoherence probability remains finite and reaches a maximum when the aperture radius is comparable to the relevant electromagnetic wavelength. Because the interaction is spatially localized, aperture-induced decoherence is generally weaker than that produced by a cylindrical hole, except for sufficiently large apertures at high temperature. Finally, we show that, for sufficiently large holes, decoherence can dominate the spatial broadening of a focused electron probe and must therefore be incorporated into the design of coherent electron-beam instruments.

</details>

**Summary.** This theoretical study analyzes the full counting statistics of fermionic particle number growth in driven quantum lattices. Using the Schwinger-Keldysh formalism, the authors derive the cumulant generating function, showing that the growth rate depends critically on the underlying lattice structure. The results distinguish between linear growth (for delocalized states) and non-linear growth (for localized states), providing a general diagnostic tool for open quantum systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a powerful, general theoretical framework for characterizing quantum fluctuations and particle transport in open quantum systems, which is highly relevant for understanding energy/particle flow in quantum devices.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper investigates the dynamics of Full Counting Statistics (FCS) for the growth of the total number of fermions in a lattice driven by a localized particle source.

**Main result.** For clean lattices with delocalized states, all cumulants grow linearly with time in the long-time limit, while localized states can lead to non-linear growth, such as logarithmic time dependence.

**Method.** The analysis employs the Schwinger-Keldysh path integral formalism within the GKSL quantum master equation framework to derive the cumulant generating function.

**Model / system.** The system is a one-dimensional non-interacting fermionic lattice subjected to a localized particle gain (source) modeled by the GKSL equation. The Hamiltonian can be generalized to include short- or long-range hopping interactions.

**Key observables.** Full Counting Statistics (FCS), characterized by the Cumulant Generating Function (CGF), $\chi(\lambda, t)$, and its cumulants ($\kappa_n$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Localized injection strength ($\Gamma$), time ($t$), and the hopping range exponent ($\alpha$). The analysis distinguishes between the long-time limit (delocalized states) and the presence of localized states.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The linear growth result assumes the underlying lattice possesses delocalized single-particle eigenstates and the thermodynamic limit ($L 	o \infty$).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the time dependence of the first three cumulants ($\kappa_1, \kappa_2, \kappa_3$), confirming linear growth for delocalized systems and showing $\ln t$ growth for disordered/localized systems.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the theory by first establishing the GKSL framework, then applying the Schwinger-Keldysh path integral formalism to derive the CGF. It analyzes both the short-time and long-time limits, contrasting the linear growth found for clean lattices with the non-linear growth observed when disorder or localization is present.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate the dynamics of full counting statistics (FCS) of the growth of the total number of fermions in a one-dimensional non-interacting lattice subjected to a localized particle gain (source) at one edge. The dynamics of the setup is modeled by the Gorini--Kossakowski--Sudarshan--Lindblad (GKSL) quantum master equation. We recast the counting problem that involves counting particle number at every lattice site to a problem where only the local injected site is involved. We employ the Schwinger-Keldysh path integral formalism within the GKSL framework and derive an analytical expression for the cumulant generating function at arbitrary times and obtain a Levitov-Lesovik type formula in the long-time limit, earlier derived for boundary driven setups in the steady-state. For clean lattices with either short- or long-range hopping, supporting single-particle delocalized eigenstates, we show that all cumulants grow linearly with time in the asymptotic regime. Our analytical results are in excellent agreement with direct numerical simulations. These findings establish a general framework for characterizing FCS and quantum fluctuations in driven open fermionic systems with localized particle injection.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper introduces a novel Si-on-SiC platform designed to efficiently couple Vanadium color centers in SiC to optical cavities. By integrating silicon nanocavities, the authors overcome the challenge of photon extraction from high-index SiC, enabling high-purity, telecom-wavelength single-photon sources suitable for quantum network applications.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work directly addresses the physical realization of solid-state quantum emitters for quantum networking, providing a concrete, scalable platform for coupling quantum information sources to optical fibers.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is achieving efficient photon extraction from Vanadium color centers embedded in Silicon Carbide (SiC) for use in quantum network nodes operating at the telecom O-band.

**Main result.** The authors successfully demonstrated a scalable Si-on-SiC platform that enables efficient zero-phonon line (ZPL) collection, achieving high-purity single-photon emission and Purcell-enhanced lifetimes.

**Method.** The research involves heterogeneous integration of silicon nanocavities onto SiC substrates, coupled with time-resolved photoluminescence measurements and charge-state repumping using external lasers.

**Model / system.** The system is a Si-on-SiC photonic platform hosting Vanadium ($	ext{V}^{4+}$) color centers in 4H-SiC. The structure couples the emitter's emission to silicon nanocavities to enhance photon collection into the telecom O-band.

**Key observables.** Zero-phonon line (ZPL) emission, Purcell-enhanced photoluminescence, single-photon emission purity, and transient spectral hole burning linewidths.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Telecom O-band ($	ext{1278–1388 nm}$), Purcell factor ($	ext{F}_{	ext{P}}$), cavity quality factor ($	ext{Q}$), and charge-repump efficiency ($95\%$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the feasibility of foundry-compatible fabrication processes and the ability to maintain the $	ext{V}^{4+}$ charge state via external repumping.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the $	ext{V}$ dopant energy levels in $	ext{SiC}$ and schematics of the optical setup, detailing the coupling mechanism between the nanocavity and the dopants.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from identifying the fundamental physical challenge (photon extraction from high-index SiC) to proposing the Si-on-SiC heterogeneous platform, demonstrating enhanced ZPL collection in ensembles, and finally isolating and characterizing single emitters.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Vanadium color centers in silicon carbide (SiC) offer telecom O-band emission, sub-microsecond optical lifetimes, and second-scale spin relaxation times, rendering them promising candidates for quantum network nodes. However, efficient photon extraction from the high-refractive-index SiC host remains challenging. Here, we introduce a silicon-on-SiC heterogeneous photonic platform in which silicon nanocavities evanescently couple to shallow vanadium dopants in commercial 4H-SiC, enabling efficient zero-phonon line (ZPL) collection under resonant excitation. In as-grown ensembles, we observe Purcell-enhanced photoluminescence with transient spectral hole burning linewidths of 50 MHz on microsecond timescales. In dilute implanted samples, we isolate individual vanadium centers with high-purity single photon emission and a Purcell-enhanced lifetime of 109 ns. The entire optical interface operates through a single lensed fiber, including a 905 nm repump laser that recovers the vanadium charge state with 95% efficiency. These results establish Si-on-SiC as a scalable, foundry-compatible platform for telecom-wavelength spin-photon interfaces.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes ultracold bosons in a cavity-coupled Bose-Hubbard model using a projection operator technique to account for quantum fluctuations. The study maps out the phase diagram and simulates quench dynamics, demonstrating that quantum fluctuations significantly alter phase boundaries and introduce characteristic single-frequency oscillations near quantum critical points compared to mean-field predictions.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant as it tackles the complex interplay between quantum fluctuations, long-range interactions, and non-equilibrium dynamics in systems relevant to quantum simulation using ultracold atoms in optical lattices.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the equilibrium phases and non-equilibrium dynamics of ultracold bosons coupled to a cavity, specifically focusing on the role of short-range quantum fluctuations.

**Main result.** Quantum fluctuations significantly modify the phase boundaries between SF, SS, CDW, and MI phases, and the dynamics near the critical point exhibit single-frequency oscillations distinct from mean-field predictions.

**Method.** The authors employ a projection operator technique, which systematically eliminates high-energy virtual hopping processes, combined with mean-field theory for the long-range cavity interaction.

**Model / system.** The system is modeled by ultracold bosons in a two-dimensional (2D) Bose-Hubbard model coupled to a high-finesse cavity, resulting in an extended Bose-Hubbard model.

**Key observables.** Superfluid (SF), Supersolid (SS), Charge-Density-Wave (CDW), and Mott Insulating (MI) phases; time evolution of superfluid order parameters and characteristic oscillation frequencies.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Hopping amplitude (J), on-site repulsion (U), cavity-mediated interaction strength (V), and quench/ramp rates.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The method captures only short-range quantum fluctuations over mean-field theory and does not capture Kibble-Zurek scaling during ramps across critical points.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare the time evolution of the order parameter $|\Delta_A(t)|$ for quenches near the critical point (showing single-frequency oscillations) versus deep in the SF regime (showing multi-frequency dynamics), contrasting the projection operator method with mean-field theory.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the Hamiltonian and the atomic limit, develops the theoretical framework using the projection operator formalism for the ground state phase diagram, and finally analyzes non-equilibrium dynamics via quench and ramp simulations.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We employ a projection operator technique to study the equilibrium phases and the non-equilibrium quench and ramp dynamics of ultracold bosons described by a two-dimensional (2D) Bose-Hubbard model coupled to a high-finesse cavity with competing local short-range and cavity-mediated long-range interactions. Our analysis relies on a systematic elimination of high-energy virtual hopping processes; this enables us to capture the effects of short-range quantum fluctuations on the phase diagram of the model while treating the cavity-induced long-range interaction within mean-field theory. We find that the phase boundaries between the superfluid (SF), supersolid (SS), charge-density-wave (CDW) and Mott insulating (MI) phases are significantly modified by the presence of these fluctuations. We use this approach to study the dynamics of bosons following a quench/ramp from the CDW to the SS and SF phases; our analysis indicates the presence of oscillatory dynamics characterized by a single frequency due to a quench which takes the system near the critical point. In contrast, for a quench deep inside the SF phase, the dynamics involves multiple frequencies. An explicit comparison with Gutzwiller mean-field theory shows the importance of quantum fluctuations in shaping such post-quench dynamics; this feature may be tested experimentally as we discuss. We also study the ramp dynamics of these bosons and identify a bound on the ramp rate above which the present method is expected to produce accurate results.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes the stability of time-crystal order in a disordered kicked Ising model under various driving protocols. It finds that interactions offer protection against dephasing for periodic drives but destabilize multipolar drives, while also revealing a geometry-dependent 'coordination gain' not predicted by simple tilt measurements. The findings advance understanding of decoherence mechanisms in periodically driven quantum matter.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides detailed insights into how local disorder and structured interactions compete with environmental decoherence in non-equilibrium quantum many-body systems, which is highly relevant to understanding quantum computation stability.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates how different types of interactions affect the coherence time of time-crystal order in periodically driven quantum systems, particularly comparing periodic versus random multipolar drives.

**Main result.** Stronger interactions protect time-crystal order against dephasing from periodic drives but destabilize it under random multipolar drives, and coordination effects beyond total interaction strength are measurable.

**Method.** The research employs exact diagonalization (ED) simulations and Matrix-Product-State (MPS) time evolution to analyze the dynamics of a disordered kicked Ising model.

**Model / system.** The system is a disordered kicked Ising model of spin-1/2 sites, driven by periodic or random multipolar sequences, and subjected to per-site dephasing ($\gamma$).

**Key observables.** Coherence time ($T_c$), transverse tilt ($	heta^2_\perp$), and ratios of coherence times across different drive types and lattice geometries.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The disorder strength ($D$), the coupling strength ($J$), the dephasing rate ($\gamma$), and the drive order ($n=0, 1, 2$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The initial state is assumed to be fully polarized; the coherence time definition is sensitive, requiring multiple checks for robustness.

**Figures summary.** Figures summarize the periodic tilt, block residuals, and measured ratios of coherence times for $N=16$, while tables show disorder scan results for $T_c$ ratios.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically compares the coherence time scaling for periodic drives versus multipolar drives, analyzes the role of geometry (grid vs. ring) at fixed interaction strength, and discusses the underlying 'toggling-frame' picture.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We show that stronger interactions protect periodically driven time-crystal order against dephasing but destabilise order under random multipolar drives, and that coordination matters beyond the total interaction strength. We studied a disordered kicked Ising model of $N=12$ and $16$ spins with imperfect $π$ pulses and per-site dephasing by exact diagonalisation, comparing a periodic drive, random multipolar drives of order $n=0,1,2$ and the Thue-Morse sequence, and separated coupling strength from coordination by comparing a grid with a ring at equal total interaction strength $zJ$. For the periodic drive the coherence time scales approximately as $1/γ$, and stronger coupling reduces the transverse tilt on which dephasing acts. For multipolar drives of order $n\ge1$, doubling the coupling on a ring shortens the coherence time to $0.54$ ($n=1$), $0.37$ ($n=2$) and $0.44$ (Thue-Morse) at $N=16$, while random signs ($n=0$) are unaffected. A disorder scan supports a toggling-frame picture in which interactions spoil the block cancellation of the pulse error. At equal $zJ$ the grid outlives the ring by $2.15$ ($N=12$) and $2.78$ ($N=16$) for the periodic drive despite an identical transverse tilt, a coordination effect beyond this picture. All ratios hold under three definitions of the coherence time.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper proposes a breakthrough detection method for axion dark matter using a phase-resolved haloscope. Instead of measuring excess power, the technique measures the phase shift induced by the axion field via coupling to a tunable gyromagnetic mode. This approach promises significantly enhanced sensitivity and a vastly expanded search range compared to current state-of-the-art detectors.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems as it proposes a novel measurement scheme that moves beyond simple power detection to utilize phase information in a superconducting cavity QED setup.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary goal is to develop a quantum-enhanced, phase-resolved protocol for detecting extremely weak axion dark matter signals, overcoming the limitations of conventional power-measurement haloscopes.

**Main result.** The proposed phase-resolved haloscope technique promises improvements of at least 4 orders of magnitude in figure of merit and 2 orders of magnitude in mass window compared to standard haloscopes.

**Method.** The method involves measuring the axion amplitude and phase directly using an interferometric protocol, which translates the axion interaction into a measurable frequency shift rather than just an excess power.

**Model / system.** The system utilizes a non-linear cavity coupled to a magnetic crystal hosting 'gyromagnetic modes' ($\hat{m}$). The dynamics are analyzed using the Keldysh path integral technique to derive an effective action for the readout mode.

**Key observables.** The key observable is the phase shift (frequency shift, $\Delta\omega_a$) in the readout cavity, which depends on the phase difference between the axion and the gyromagnetic mode.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Key parameters include the axion-photon coupling constant ($g_{a\gamma\gamma}$), the coupling strengths ($K_{am}$), and the achievable figure of merit ($F_{phase}$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the semiclassical approximation and assumes the gyromagnetic mode is hosted by a magnetic chiral crystal like YIG.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the comparison between conventional (power-based) and phase-resolved (phase-based) haloscopes, showing the superior sensitivity and tunability of the proposed method.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the general Hamiltonian, then deriving the phase-resolved signal mechanism via the Keldysh path integral, and finally quantifying the performance improvement by comparing the figure of merit ($F_{phase}$) against conventional benchmarks.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We propose a paradigm for quantum enhanced axion dark matter search, which does not rely on power measurements. We propose to measure directly the axion amplitude and phase in an interferometric protocol at the quantum limit, using a non-linear cavity. In addition, we introduce gyromagnetic modes as wide mass range transducers for axion signals compatible with standard haloscope designs. We expect this scheme to offer an improvement of at least 4 orders of magnitude in figure of merit and at least 2 orders of magnitude in mass window with respect to standard haloscopes. Owing to its generality, our proposed protocol has the potential to speed up axion search but also the search for dark photons or other cosmological objects, such as galactic masers.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper theoretically investigates how an impurity particle forms a quasiparticle, or polaron, when immersed in a Bose gas undergoing a Mott-Insulator to Superfluid transition. Using a variational approach, the authors map out the polaron's structure and dynamics, showing that strong correlations near the critical point lead to unique, measurable features in its spectral properties and time evolution.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides detailed, quantitative predictions for how local impurities interact with strongly correlated quantum fluids, offering a theoretical framework applicable to ultracold atomic experiments in optical lattices.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study focuses on developing a unified description of a mobile impurity particle (polaron) immersed in a quantum degenerate Bose gas as it undergoes a phase transition from a Mott Insulator (MI) to a Superfluid (SF) state.

**Main result.** The impurity forms various polaron and molecular states, exhibiting non-analytic features near the quantum critical point, and the system's dynamics are strongly dictated by the surrounding bosonic phase.

**Method.** The authors employ a multi-mode variational ansatz based on the quantum Gutzwiller approach, solving a generalized eigenvalue problem derived from the Bose-Hubbard model Hamiltonian.

**Model / system.** The system models an impurity interacting with a bath of bosons described by the 2D Bose-Hubbard model, characterized by hopping (J), on-site repulsion (U), and impurity-boson interaction ($U_{IB}$).

**Key observables.** Impurity spectral function, real space impurity-boson density correlation function $G(r)$, and non-equilibrium Ramsey contrast $|A(t)|$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The ratio of interaction strengths ($U_{IB}/U$) and the ratio of hopping to repulsion ($J/U$), particularly near the quantum critical point (QCP).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on a variational ansatz truncated to include up to two excitations of the bosons, and the time evolution is calculated using time-stepped Arnoldi/Lanczos methods.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the impurity spectral function across different interaction regimes, and plots show the dependence of wave function components and density correlations on the interaction strength, highlighting changes at the QCP.

**Paper structure.** The paper systematically analyzes the ground state structure (spectral properties, density correlations) and the non-equilibrium dynamics (Ramsey contrast) of the polaron across the MI-SF transition, detailing how the underlying bosonic phase dictates the quasiparticle behavior.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

A mobile impurity particle immersed in a quantum degenerate gas leads to the formation of a quasiparticle, which can   serve as a sensor for its environment. Here, we develop a unified wave function description of an impurity in a two-dimensional Bose-Hubbard model across the Mott-insulator to superfluid transition. Using a multi-mode variational ansatz based on the quantum Gutzwiller approach, we show that   the impurity can form several kinds of polaronic and molecular states. In addition to their spectral properties, the   wave function provides direct access to the microscopic structure of these states, and we demonstrate that strong correlations in the critical regime of the quantum phase transition give rise to several non-analytic features in the polaron properties. Increasing the impurity-boson interaction leads to transitions between polaron and molecular ground states, and the number of bosons in the impurity dressing cloud grows rapidly at the quantum critical point as the bath modes soften. We furthermore reveal qualitatively distinct non-equilibrium many-body dynamics after the injection of the impurity in the different phases of the Bose-Hubbard model. Our spectral, real space, and dynamical predictions describe complementary properties of   polarons in a strongly correlated bosonic bath, which can be observed using current techniques with atoms in optical lattices.

</details>

**Summary.** This work shows that critical behavior in an Ising spin system can arise purely from memory-dependent connectivity rules, bypassing the need for temperature or explicit energy dynamics. By tuning a connectivity parameter $\alpha$, the system undergoes a transition marked by spontaneous symmetry breaking and singular energy responses. This reveals a novel route to understanding non-equilibrium criticality in many-body systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** It provides a non-equilibrium mechanism for criticality, which is highly relevant for understanding complex dynamics in open quantum systems where thermal baths or simple Hamiltonians might not fully capture the physics.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper demonstrates that critical-like collective behavior can emerge in an Ising spin system without relying on temperature or energy-based dynamics.

**Main result.** Memory-dependent connectivity alone can generate collective critical behavior, evidenced by singular responses in energy derivatives and the emergence of spontaneous symmetry breaking as a control parameter is varied.

**Method.** The authors use numerical simulations to analyze the system's evolution by varying a connectivity strength parameter ($\alpha$) and observing changes in magnetization distributions and cluster-size statistics.

**Model / system.** The system is an Ising spin model on a square lattice whose dynamics are governed by a Quiet-Time Cluster Model (QTCM). This dynamics is memory-dependent, controlled by the time elapsed since each spin was last updated, and is decoupled from the Ising Hamiltonian.

**Key observables.** Magnetization ($m$), Ising Energy ($E$), and the cluster-size distribution ($n(s)$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The connectivity strength parameter $\alpha$, which drives the system through different collective regimes.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The dynamics are assumed to be driven solely by the local quiet-time variable, and the Ising Hamiltonian only enters as a post-hoc observable.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the evolution of magnetization distributions (from $\delta$-like to multi-peaked) and the cluster-size distribution (showing power-law regimes) as the parameter $\alpha$ is tuned, highlighting the critical point $\alpha_c$.

**Paper structure.** The paper introduces the QTCM dynamics, analyzes the system's response to varying $\alpha$ by examining magnetization and energy, and concludes by showing that memory effects alone can induce critical phenomena, bypassing the need for thermal or energy-based driving.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Criticality in the Ising model is conventionally generated by Hamiltonian dynamics and controlled by temperature. Here we show that critical like behavior can emerge in an Ising system whose dynamics is completely independent of the Ising Hamiltonian and contains no temperature like parameter. We introduce an adaptive cluster dynamics in which spin connectivity is controlled by a local quiet time variable, the time elapsed since a spin was last updated. The Ising Hamiltonian enters only as an observable characterizing the resulting configurations. As the parameter $α$, controlling the connectivity strength, is varied, the system undergoes spontaneous symmetry breaking accompanied by strong collective fluctuations. The cluster size distribution develops an extended power law regime, terminated by a small finite size hump at the largest scales, while the Ising energy exhibits a singular response to the variation of $α$. These results show that memory dependent connectivity alone can generate collective critical behavior, revealing a route to nonequilibrium criticality without energy based dynamics.

</details>

**Summary.** This research investigates topological edge states in the anisotropic quantum Rabi model using trapped-ion quantum simulators. The authors overcome the challenge of distinguishing edge states from bulk states when periodicity is broken by analyzing intrinsic quantum signatures. They successfully identify the topological edge state by measuring its unique chirality and spin-boson separability, providing a powerful, experimentally verifiable method for probing topological physics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete, measurable protocol for detecting topological phases in quantum simulators by moving beyond simple localization arguments to use intrinsic quantum correlations like chirality and entanglement structure.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The primary challenge is distinguishing topological edge states (TES) from localized bulk states when the system lacks translational periodicity, making spatial localization an insufficient diagnostic tool.

**Main result.** The TES can be robustly identified by its intrinsic topological signatures, specifically exhibiting well-defined chirality and near-complete spin-boson separability, which contrasts sharply with the bulk states.

**Method.** The study employs adiabatic state preparation and characterization using trapped-ion quantum simulators to measure multiple quantum diagnostics.

**Model / system.** The system is the Anisotropic Quantum Rabi Model (AQRM) simulated using trapped $^{171}	ext{Yb}^+$ ions. The model involves coupling between spin and bosonic (motional) degrees of freedom.

**Key observables.** Chirality ($\langle\hat{\Xi}angle$), spin-boson separability (quantified by second-order Rényi entropy $S_{2,	ext{spin}}$), and the bosonic component's phase-space distribution (squeezed vacuum state).

**Important parameters / regimes.** The relative coupling strength $g_r = g_2/g_1$ dictates the topological phase ($g_r < 1$ for TES) versus the trivial phase ($g_r > 1$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the ability to measure expectation values in the even-parity subspace, and the experiment uses trapped $^{171}	ext{Yb}^+$ ions.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate parity-resolved energy spectra showing the zero-energy TES, joint spin-Fock populations and chirality distinguishing TES from bulk states, and the characteristic function of the bosonic subsystem.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the theoretical framework and diagnostics (chirality, separability) for distinguishing TES. It then details the experimental implementation using trapped ions, measuring these diagnostics across different coupling regimes to confirm the topological characterization.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Topological phases are governed by discrete symmetries that protect boundary modes against local perturbations. When translational periodicity is absent, the bulk states also become localized, so that a topological edge state can no longer be distinguished from them by spatial localization alone. Here, we investigate the topological edge state (TES) and bulk eigenstates of the anisotropic quantum Rabi model (AQRM) in a trapped-ion quantum simulator. The AQRM hosts a topological phase in a one-dimensional synthetic lattice, whose translational symmetry is broken by the non-uniform couplings scaling with the site index. While both the TES and bulk states show localized distributions, we find that the TES exhibits well-defined chirality and near-complete spin--boson separability as signatures of the topological phase, in contrast to the bulk states. Phase-space tomography further reveals that the bosonic component of the TES is a squeezed vacuum state, with squeezing up to 6.45 dB. These results identify the TES through its intrinsic topological signatures and establish eigenstate-level characterization as a route to probing topological phenomena.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper reports the design and experimental realization of a metasurface on $	ext{NbOCl}_2$ to generate polarization-entangled photon pairs. By exploiting the material's inherent optical anisotropy, the metasurface is engineered to balance the nonlinear coupling pathways, achieving a high-fidelity entangled state source. This establishes a powerful, scalable platform for quantum photonics.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete, scalable platform (vdW metasurfaces) for realizing quantum light sources, moving beyond bulk crystals and directly addressing the engineering challenge of controlling quantum interactions in solid-state systems.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The challenge is to create compact, controllable sources for polarization-entangled photon pairs, which are crucial resources for quantum information technologies.

**Main result.** The authors successfully demonstrated the generation of polarization-entangled Bell states with a measured fidelity up to 92% using a specially engineered metasurface.

**Method.** They engineered a resonant metasurface on a van der Waals material ($	ext{NbOCl}_2$) to manipulate its intrinsic optical anisotropy, thereby controlling the nonlinear susceptibility tensor for Spontaneous Parametric Down-Conversion (SPDC).

**Model / system.** The physical system is a resonant vdW nonlinear metasurface patterned on $	ext{NbOCl}_2$. The engineering exploits the material's inherent optical anisotropy to selectively enhance and balance the nonlinear coupling pathways ($\chi^{(2)}$) responsible for generating entangled pairs.

**Key observables.** Measured state fidelity (up to 92%), concurrence ($0.91 \pm 0.04$), and the ratio of nonlinear susceptibilities ($\chi_{HVV}^{(2)	ext{eff}} / \chi_{HHH}^{(2)	ext{eff}}$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Metasurface dimensions ($p = 450 	ext{ nm}$, $d = 115 	ext{ nm}$), resonance shifts ($\sim 106 	ext{ meV}$), and the required spectral overlap for balanced SPDC.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The primary assumption is that metasurface engineering can effectively control the effective nonlinear susceptibility tensor ($\chi^{(2)}$) to balance the two orthogonal polarization channels.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the concept of Bell state generation via SPDC, show angle-dependent transmission spectra revealing anisotropic resonances, and present the calculated/measured entanglement fidelity and density matrix components.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from identifying the need for controllable entangled sources to detailing the metasurface design, simulating the anisotropic optical response (FDTD), demonstrating the nonlinear enhancement (SHG), and finally characterizing the generated quantum state via coincidence measurements and polarization tomography.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Polarization-entangled photon pairs are essential resources for quantum information technologies, yet realizing compact sources with intrinsically controllable entanglement remains challenging. Van der Waals (vdW) nonlinear materials such as NbOCl2 provide atomically thin platforms for quantum light generation, yet their native crystalline anisotropies as natural materials impose limitations on accessible quantum states. Here, we develop a resonant vdW nonlinear metasurface based on NbOCl2 that exploits its intrinsic optical anisotropy to engineer polarization-dependent nonlinear responses. The anisotropic optical dispersion enables selective manipulation of resonant modes, resulting in a three-order-of-magnitude enhancement of the nonlinear response along the c axis. By further tailoring these resonant modes, we redistribute the effective second-order nonlinear susceptibility tensor between orthogonal polarization channels, balancing the spontaneous parametric down-conversion pathways along the b and c axes. This enables polarization-entangled photon generation with a measured fidelity of up to 92%. Our work establishes metasurface-enabled nonlinear optical engineering as a strategy for enhancing and controlling quantum light generation in vdW materials, providing a pathway toward scalable quantum photonic platforms.

</details>

**Summary.** This work presents a novel, highly efficient classical simulation technique for noisy Quantum Random Access Memory (QRAM) using branch pruning. By analytically predicting the evolution of 'good' quantum branches, the authors achieve substantial speedups over full simulations. This advances the practical simulation capabilities for quantum memory architectures under realistic noise models.

**Why it may be interesting.** The techniques developed for analytically predicting quantum evolution along specific, noise-avoiding paths are highly relevant for simulating open quantum systems where full time evolution is intractable.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the challenge of developing a fast and accurate classical simulation for Quantum Random Access Memory (QRAM) operating under noise, specifically amplitude damping.

**Main result.** They achieve significant computational speedups (up to 285x) by developing a branch pruning technique that analytically predicts the final states of 'good' quantum branches.

**Method.** The core method is a quantum-trajectory Monte Carlo simulation enhanced by branch pruning, which avoids full evolution for predictable paths.

**Model / system.** The system modeled is a bucket-brigade QRAM, analyzed using both qubit and qutrit encodings. Noise includes amplitude damping and depolarizing faults.

**Key observables.** End-state fidelities, speedup factors (pruned-over-full), and the in-branch infidelity (second order in the damping rate $\gamma$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Amplitude damping strength ($\gamma$), address size ($n$), and noise probability ($\epsilon$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** The predictability of good branches under amplitude damping was not automatic, requiring novel analytical treatments for both qutrit and qubit cases.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 conceptually shows the pruned simulation for qubit-encoded QRAM using the XOR mirror. Figure 4 plots the speedup and evolved fraction versus noise level and address size.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the need for efficient simulation under damping, then details the analytical predictability for qutrit and qubit encodings, proposes a revised pruning criterion, and finally validates the entire algorithm using end-to-end benchmarks and cross-checks against density matrix evolution.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Classical simulation of quantum random access memory (QRAM) under noise can be accelerated dramatically by branch pruning: noise histories are sampled as trajectory ensembles, and good branches, whose routing paths avoid every sampled fault, need not be evolved because their final states are analytically predictable. Under amplitude damping this predictability is not automatic, because the no-jump operator $K_0$ acts on every branch at every time slice. Here we give a complete account of damping-channel predictability in bucket-brigade QRAM simulation, for both qutrit and qubit encodings. For the qutrit encoding, $K_0$ is diagonal in the node basis, and the wait state $|W\rangle$ is its fixed point, so a good branch follows the noiseless orbit up to a scalar attenuation. In the qubit encoding, phase-kickback memory fetching between two Hadamard walls makes $K_0$ no longer diagonal, yet the resulting structure is exactly solvable in closed form. Conditional on no jump, the in-branch infidelity of a good branch is second order in the damping rate $γ$, with coherent leakage $\sim n^2γ^2/4$ per data qubit, and the closed form captures it without approximation. We also revise the pruning criterion for the qubit encoding. The resulting algorithm evolves only the bad branches plus one reference branch and shares every other cost with the full evolution it replaces. It is validated by end-to-end benchmarks with pruned-over-full speedups up to $285\times$ and by trajectory-level tests confirming every closed form to machine precision.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper analyzes three-component Hubbard models under a transverse field, developing a generalized $\eta$-pairing concept to find exact eigenstates despite symmetry breaking. The authors construct a specific tensor-product state whose dynamics exhibit quantum many-body scarring and long-range order. The work is significant for establishing new theoretical tools to describe correlated electron systems beyond conventional pairing symmetries.

**Why it may be interesting.** The work extends pairing concepts (like $\eta$-pairing) to multi-component systems where symmetry is broken, providing a theoretical framework for understanding exotic correlated phases in complex quantum materials.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The study investigates the existence and properties of exact eigenstates in three-component Hubbard models subjected to a transverse field, particularly concerning generalized $\eta$-pairing symmetry.

**Main result.** The authors constructed exact eigenstates exhibiting off-diagonal long-range order and developed a tensor-product state whose dynamics realize quantum many-body scar dynamics with long-range magnetic order.

**Method.** The research employs the restricted spectrum-generating algebra (RSGA) to construct the exact eigenstates and analyzes state preparation using quench dynamics, comparing perturbative and exact time evolution.

**Model / system.** The system is a three-component Hubbard model on a bipartite lattice, governed by a Hamiltonian including on-site interactions, hopping, and a transverse field term that breaks component number conservation.

**Key observables.** Off-diagonal long-range order (ODLRO), fidelity $F(t)$ approaching unity, and the existence of three equally spaced energy towers.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The transverse field strength ($\Sigma_x^j$), chemical potential ($\mu$), and resonant conditions are key parameters.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis relies on the generalized $\eta$-pairing operators generating exact eigenstates via the RSGA, and the state preparation analysis compares perturbative approximations to full exact time evolution.

**Figures summary.** Figure 1 compares the fidelity dynamics $F(t)$ for both vacuum and maximally mixed initial states, showing that the fidelity approaches unity, confirming robust state preparation.

**Paper structure.** The paper first establishes the theoretical framework by introducing the generalized $\eta$-pairing operator and using RSGA to find exact eigenstates. It then constructs an exact tensor-product state and discusses its periodic dynamics. Finally, it proposes and verifies three quench protocols for preparing this state, analyzing the dynamics using fidelity measures.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We investigate three-component Hubbard models on a bipartite lattice in the presence of a trans?verse field. Unlike the two-component Hubbard model, where the η-pairing symmetry survives the transverse field, the three-component model possesses neither η-pairing symmetry nor conservation of the particle number of each component. We introduce a generalized η-pairing operator, formed as a hybridization of three types of two-component pairing operators, and employ the restricted spectrum-generating algebra to construct a family of exact eigenstates. These eigenstates exhibit off-diagonal long-range order. Furthermore, we construct an exact tensor-product state whose co?herent periodic dynamics provide an exact realization of quantum many-body scar dynamics while simultaneously exhibiting long-range magnetic order. We also propose three protocols for preparing this state via quench dynamics, and verify their effectiveness through numerical simulations.

</details>

**Summary.** This work investigates how Ising systems behave when rapidly quenched across a first-order magnetic phase transition. The authors find that the system undergoes a dynamic percolation transition at a finite time $t_c(h)$. This percolation event is shown to be intimately linked to the spinodal instability of the magnetization, suggesting a general mechanism for non-equilibrium transitions in such systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** The connection drawn between dynamic percolation and spinodal decomposition in the context of first-order phase transitions is a powerful tool for understanding non-equilibrium dynamics in many-body systems, relevant for quench dynamics in quantum simulation.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper analyzes the out-of-equilibrium relaxational dynamics of ferromagnetic Ising-like systems driven across their low-temperature magnetic first-order transition (FOT) line.

**Main result.** It shows the emergence of a dynamic percolation transition at a finite critical time $t_c(h)$, which relates the percolation critical behavior to the spinodal-like exponential dependence of the magnetization in the small-$h$ limit.

**Method.** The study uses Monte Carlo simulations to track the time evolution of spin clusters and analyze finite-size scaling behavior across the quench.

**Model / system.** The model is a two-dimensional Ising system on a square lattice governed by a Hamiltonian including an external magnetic field $h$. The dynamics are studied using relaxational Monte Carlo simulations.

**Key observables.** Magnetization $M(t)$, the size of the largest positive and negative spin clusters ($\Sigma_{\pm}(t)$), and the critical time $t_c(h)$.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The external magnetic field $h$, the quench protocol (sudden vs. slow variation), and the system size $L$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis focuses on the large-volume limit ($V 	o \infty$) and assumes the dynamics are governed by relaxational processes.

**Figures summary.** The notes mention figures showing the time evolution of cluster sizes ($\Sigma_+(t)$ and $\Sigma_-(t)$) and the scaling behavior of these observables near the transition time $t_c$.

**Paper structure.** The paper analyzes the dynamics by first setting up the model and quench protocol, then identifying the percolation transition via cluster analysis, and finally relating the critical time scaling to the spinodal behavior of the magnetization.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

We analyze the out-of-equilibrium relaxational dynamics of ferromagnetic Ising-like systems driven across their low-temperature magnetic first-order transition (FOT) line, by sudden and slow variations of an external homogenous magnetic field $h$. As a paradigmatic example, we consider a two-dimensional Ising system driven across its low-temperature FOT line by suddently quenching $h$ from $h_i<0$ to $h>0$, inducing a transition from the negatively to the positively magnetized phase. We show the emergence of a dynamic percolation transition at a finite critical time $t_c(h)$ along the post-quench evolution for finite (sufficiently small) values of $h$, which is marked by the percolation of the largest positive-spin cluster and the antipercolation of the largest negative-spin cluster. This out-of-equilibrium percolation transition displays a finite-size scaling behavior as in the standard random-percolation case. However, while the fractal dimension of the percolating clusters is consistent with the random-percolation value, the exponent controlling the approach to criticality differs and depends on $h$. We also show that the percolation transition marks the passage from the metastable negatively-magnetized phase to the stable positively-magnetized one. Therefore, in the small-$h$ limit, the percolation critical behavior is related to the spinodal-like behavior of the magnetization, implying that the percolation time $t_c(h)$ exhibits a spinodal-like exponential dependence on $h$. The existence of percolation transitions is likely a generic phenomenon at magnetic Ising-like FOTs. For example, we observe an analogous behavior in dynamic (Kibble-Zurek-like) protocols entailing slow variations of the magnetic field driving the crossing of the FOT line.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper demonstrates how the spatial structure of the pump beam, using higher-order HG and LG modes, can nonlinearly engineer the Hong-Ou-Mandel interference effect. By controlling the pump's parity and orbital angular momentum, the authors achieve enhanced sensitivity in the HOM interference signal, opening pathways for quantum-enhanced rotation sensing.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work is highly relevant to quantum optics and open quantum systems, as it demonstrates a method to engineer quantum interference effects (HOM) using structured light, which can be viewed as a form of quantum state engineering for sensing applications.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper addresses the nonlinear engineering of Hong-Ou-Mandel (HOM) interference by controlling the spatial symmetry of the input photon pairs using structured light.

**Main result.** The HOM interference pattern exhibits rich, predictable structures dependent on the parity and orbital angular momentum content of the structured pump light, enabling enhanced angular resolution sensing.

**Method.** The authors combine theoretical derivations using creation operators and Wigner small-d matrix formalism with experimental implementation using Spatial Light Modulators (SLMs) to shape the pump beam.

**Model / system.** The system involves generating degenerate photon pairs via Spontaneous Parametric Down-Conversion (SPDC) and analyzing their interference at a beam-splitter using structured light modes, specifically Hermite-Gaussian (HG) and Laguerre-Gaussian (LG) beams.

**Key observables.** HOM coincidence probability ($P_{	ext{coinc}}$) as a function of pump rotation angle ($	heta$), and the visibility of the interference dip/peak.

**Important parameters / regimes.** Pump mode order ($n, \ell$), pump rotation angle ($	heta$), and the orbital angular momentum content ($\ell$).

**Assumptions / limitations.** Assumes paraxial pump and monochromatic SPDC, and that the analysis for HG modes is independent of the index $m$ (sensitive only to parity along $x$).

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the spatial symmetry of HG modes, the angular dependence of HOM interference for various HG and LG petal modes, and the schematic experimental setup.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from establishing the theoretical basis of HOM interference control via pump parity, to demonstrating this effect using HG modes, and finally extending the concept to LG petal modes to show enhanced rotational sensing capabilities.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

A pair of photons entering a Hong-Ou-Mandel interferometer will bunch or anti-bunch depending on the symmetry of their state in the measured degree of freedom, resulting in constructive or destructive interference. For photon pairs generated through spontaneous parametric down-conversion, this symmetry can be engineered through linear transformations and projections applied to the photon pairs, or by tailoring the pump field. Here, we adopt the latter approach to demonstrate that the pump's parity affects the shape and frequency of the transition from constructive to destructive interference. We demonstrate this concept theoretically and experimentally using a rotating structured pump mode encoded in the Hermite-Gaussian and Laguerre-Gaussian bases. In the former case, we show that the transition exhibits a rich structure unique to the mode family, resulting in enhanced sensitivity as the mode order increases. In the latter case, we demonstrate, as with NOON states, an integer enhancement in angular resolution by a factor proportional to the orbital angular momentum content, thereby opening the possibility of Hong-Ou-Mandel-enhanced rotation sensing.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper critically examines the 'collapse postulate' of quantum mechanics, arguing it is inconsistent with relativistic principles like causality and localization. It proposes an 'ensemble interpretation' as a more natural framework that explains quantum phenomena, such as interference, without invoking instantaneous wave function collapses.

**Why it may be interesting.** This is highly relevant as it tackles the foundational interpretation of quantum mechanics, which underpins all advanced topics in quantum physics, including open quantum systems and measurement theory.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper questions the fundamental validity of the quantum mechanical 'collapse postulate' when reconciling quantum mechanics with special relativity and localization principles.

**Main result.** The collapse postulate is shown to be inconsistent with fundamental principles like causality and localization limits derived from special relativity, suggesting an alternative ensemble interpretation is necessary.

**Method.** The analysis compares the predictions of the standard collapse interpretation against those derived from the unitary Schrödinger Equation evolution, using the two-slit experiment as a primary test case.

**Model / system.** The discussion centers on quantum particles and fields, using the two-slit experiment and the mathematical framework of wave function evolution (Schrödinger Equation) versus instantaneous state jumps (collapse postulate).

**Key observables.** Interference patterns, wavefunction localization, and the probability of measurement outcomes.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The assumptions of special relativity and the requirement for causality are central constraints.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The paper critiques the assumption that the collapse postulate is a fundamental, necessary component of quantum mechanics.

**Figures summary.** The notes reference a schematic of the two-slit experiment, illustrating the contrast between the standard collapse model and the implications of wave function behavior.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses by first establishing the conflict between localization and relativity (Hegerfeldt's theorem), then contrasting the standard collapse view with the ensemble interpretation, and finally demonstrating inconsistencies in the collapse model using experimental analogies.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Hegerfeldt's theorem shows that the localization of a particle (or field) is not possible under very general assumptions of quantum mechanics and special relativity. This theorem, and further developments and associated theorems force penetrating questions on the proper understanding of the theory and its use. In particular, the use of the collapse postulate is called into question. The existence of particles and even localized fields are called into question. And, this in turn challenges local measurements. It generally forces one to consider the profound problems and even wrong results that arise from the collapse postulate. We give a qualitatively new example of such a wrong result. Researchers and students alike are bothered by these fundamental issues. Students' ability to learn the material, and even their interest in physics, can be compromised by such disturbing conundra that seem to make physics, or at least QFT and its QM limit, seem incomprehensible and even inconsistent. This article resolves these issues in a way accessible to undergraduates, by applying the natural (minimal) interpretation of quantum mechanics (QM) (the ensemble interpretation) and explicating and clarifying the basic principles and premises used in QM and the Hegerfeldt theorem and its application to measurements.

</details>

**Summary.** This paper rigorously analyzes asymmetric readout errors in NISQ quantum computing experiments, building on previous work. By applying advanced statistical tools, the authors tested hypotheses regarding gate error contamination using data from Google's 2019 experiment. The key finding is that while some simulations show evidence of gate error effects, the primary experimental data suggests readout asymmetry is the dominant source of error, though temporal instability remains a concern.

**Why it may be interesting.** The detailed analysis of readout error characterization is crucial for understanding the limitations of current quantum hardware, directly impacting the feasibility of running complex quantum algorithms.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The paper analyzes asymmetric readout errors in Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) experiments, extending previous work that focused on symmetric errors.

**Main result.** The effect of amplitude damping gate errors, predicted by some models, was not observed in the Google 2019 experimental data for $12 \le n \le 53$ qubits, although discrepancies were found in certain simulators.

**Method.** The authors use Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) and Fourier methods to model and quantify the asymmetric readout error probabilities ($q_{1	o 0}$ and $q_{0	o 1}$).

**Model / system.** The study focuses on NISQ devices, referencing the Google 2019 'quantum supremacy' experiment and using quantum simulators (IBM's and Google's). The noise is modeled using a 3-parameter readout error model.

**Key observables.** Readout error probabilities ($q_{1	o 0}, q_{0	o 1}$), the fraction of zeroes and ones in measurement samples, and the anticoncentration measure ($c$).

**Important parameters / regimes.** Number of qubits ($n=12$ to $n=53$), and the error parameters derived from MLE.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes that the observed variation in measured proportions is primarily due to readout errors, though later sections suggest temporal instability might stem from gate errors rather than readout drift.

**Figures summary.** Figures compare measured proportions of 1's from Sycamore/Zuchongzhi against stable simulations, showing that measured variation exceeds expected binomial distributions, suggesting instability.

**Paper structure.** The paper progresses from analyzing the theoretical framework for asymmetric errors using Fourier tools, to applying this to Google's 2019 data (showing no gate error signature), and finally comparing results across multiple simulators and experimental runs to pinpoint the source of observed instability.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

This paper continues our analysis of NISQ experiments and especially the Google 2019 ``quantum supremacy" experiment. In arXiv:2008.05177 we proposed statistical tools to analyze symmetric and asymmetric readout errors, and the symmetric case was extensively developed and studied in arXiv:2404.00935, where we used Fourier methods combined with statistical tools.   Here we extend and complement our earlier study and analyze asymmetric readout errors for data from experiments and simulations.   Our study was further motivated by a paper by Fefferman et al. arXiv:2306.16659, who showed that the effect of amplitude damping gate errors is to have larger fractions of zeroes in the samples produced by the quantum computer. We show that this effect of gate errors is not observed in the Google experimental data, where, for the entire range of the number of qubits, $12 \le n \le 53$, the fraction of zeroes and ones reflects only the asymmetry of reported readout errors, and report on simulations with $n=12,14$ using IBM's and Google's simulators.

</details>

**Type:** experiment · **Category:** other · **PDF:** <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.31832v1>

The error in the mea- surement of R can be reduced arbitrarily by increasing the number of iterations performed.</sub>

**Summary.** This paper presents a novel technique to determine the intrinsic precision of a clock using only its own ticking signal and a simple electronic delay mechanism. By analyzing the statistical moments of the tick count until a delayed trigger fires, the authors derive a formula that bypasses the need for external time standards. This method is significant for developing autonomous timekeeping systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** While not strictly quantum, the concept of self-referential measurement and characterizing fundamental physical constants (like time precision) using only internal statistics is highly relevant to quantum metrology and quantum clock comparisons.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The core problem is characterizing the intrinsic precision ($R$) of a clock without relying on any external, ideal time reference or a second, equally precise clock.

**Main result.** The authors derived and experimentally validated a formula to estimate clock precision using only the statistical properties of the clock's own ticks and a delayed trigger circuit.

**Method.** The method involves connecting the clock to a signal splitter, using one output to drive a delayed trigger, and counting the ticks at the other output until the trigger fires. The precision is extracted from the mean and variance of this tick count.

**Model / system.** The system consists of a single autonomous clock, a signal splitter, and a delayed trigger circuit. The analysis treats the clock as a source of weakly dependent ticks, and the delay element's uncertainty is explicitly incorporated into the final estimator.

**Key observables.** The primary observables are the mean tick count ($E[	au_D]$) and the variance ($\Delta^2(	au_D)$) measured before the delayed trigger fires.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The key parameters are the clock precision $R = \mu^2/\sigma^2$, the average ticking period $\mu$, and the normalized uncertainty from the delay element $\Delta^2(D)/\mu^2$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The analysis assumes the asymptotic regime where the delay uncertainty is small relative to the tick count variance, and that the delayed trigger only marks the end of the interval without defining a frequency standard.

**Figures summary.** Figure 2 illustrates the block diagram of the proposed setup: the clock feeds a signal splitter, which connects to both the delayed trigger and the tick counter.

**Paper structure.** The paper develops the theoretical framework using renewal theory and central limit theorems to derive the asymptotic formula for $R$. This is followed by a detailed description of the experimental setup and validation using a microcontroller-based clock source.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

Determining a clock's precision usually requires comparison with a better time reference, yet no ideal reference is physically attainable. We show how a single clock can characterise its own precision using only a signal splitter and delayed trigger, whose uncertainty is explicitly accounted for. The resulting estimator depends only on tick-count statistics. A purpose-built electronic circuit validates the method without an external timekeeper or a second clock.

</details>

**Summary.** The authors experimentally demonstrate a protocol to implement the Cubic Phase Gate (CPG) on the motional modes of a trapped ion. By optimizing sequences of state-dependent force pulses, they achieve high-fidelity gate operations for both vacuum and coherent states. This work is significant because it realizes a necessary anharmonic nonlinearity required for universal quantum computation in continuous-variable systems.

**Why it may be interesting.** This work provides a concrete, high-fidelity experimental realization of a non-Gaussian, anharmonic gate (CPG) using trapped ions, which is a crucial building block for scaling up CV quantum computation beyond simple linear operations.

<details><summary>Detailed structure</summary>

**Main problem.** The central goal is to experimentally demonstrate and characterize the Cubic Phase Gate (CPG), which is a required anharmonic nonlinear unitary for achieving universal gate sets in Continuous-Variable (CV) quantum computation.

**Main result.** The protocol successfully approximates the CPG for both vacuum and low-amplitude coherent state inputs, achieving high state overlaps (up to 0.998) and demonstrating nonlinear squeezing below the vacuum limit.

**Method.** The CPG is approximated by implementing a sequence of state-dependent force (SDF) pulses, with parameters optimized numerically to maximize the state overlap with the target unitary evolution.

**Model / system.** The experiment uses a single trapped $^{171}	ext{Yb}^+$ ion, utilizing its motional modes (specifically the R1 mode) as the quantum resource. The gate operation is implemented via controlled interactions derived from the ion's motional Hamiltonian.

**Key observables.** State overlap (fidelity), Wigner function, and Nonlinear Squeezing (NLS) of the characteristic function.

**Important parameters / regimes.** The number of pulses ($N=6, 10, 14$), initial coherent state amplitude ($|\alpha| \lesssim 0.5$), and the squeezing parameter $\lambda$.

**Assumptions / limitations.** The fidelity analysis relies on approximating the target unitary via a finite Fourier series expansion using the SDF pulses; NLS analysis requires fitting the experimental characteristic function to a theoretical model.

**Figures summary.** Figures illustrate the experimental circuit diagram, and supplementary figures compare simulated and measured Wigner functions and NLS curves for both vacuum and cubic phase states.

**Paper structure.** The paper details the theoretical requirement for anharmonic gates, presents the experimental protocol using optimized SDF pulses, and concludes with detailed characterization of the resulting state using Wigner functions and NLS measurements.

</details>

<details><summary>Abstract</summary>

The motional modes of trapped ions are promising candidates for continuous-variable (CV) quantum computation and simulation. However, to achieve a universal gate set for CV quantum computation, anharmonic nonlinear unitaries are required. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a protocol that allows us to approximate the cubic phase gate. By numerically optimizing the phase angles and amplitudes of a set of state-dependent force pulses, we demonstrate the cubic phase gate for both vacuum and low-$α$ coherent state inputs and verify its performance. Our protocol can also be extended to approximate other nonlinear unitaries.

</details>
